_comment: Spike fixture for the Fixtures pane (sb-9z3). SIBLING FILE, not a section
inside the document fixtures - the shape decision, and why:
A document fixture is an ADR-0001 envelope, and the spike's fromJson/1
mirrors the real decoder's strictness: it refuses a key the encoder would
never have written. The existing '_comment' keys already have to be
stripped before decoding for exactly that reason. Adding a 'runs' key to
the envelope would mean either a second thing to strip on every load or a
laxer decoder, and the strict check is what keeps encode(decode(b)) == b
honest. A run is also not part of the document: it is a fixture ABOUT one,
it has its own lifetime, and a host that ships documents from a database
will keep its fixtures somewhere else entirely. So: one file, keyed by
document id, fetched beside the document.
EVERYTHING HERE IS MOCKED, per the campaign's D4 ruling: a run is a scripted
sequence an author wrote, and a truth table's expected values are typed in.
Nothing in the spike interprets a chart or evaluates a predicate. The runner
REPLAYS; it does not compute. The pane says so on screen, because a fixture
UI that looks like it is running the chart would be the single most
misleading thing this spike could ship.
Every block id referenced here exists in the matching document, and every
datamodel path in a binding or a delta resolves in ../datamodel.json.
THE STEP SCHEMA every run in this file shares (card-processing and
signup-wizard alike):
label:   what the step is, in an author's words
active:  block ids the step lights on the canvas - a SET, because a
parallel region lights more than one at a time
event?:  the event name that arrived, when the step is one an event
drives (run_su_declined's raise-and-catch pair uses it twice)
note?:   prose shown under the step, for what the ids cannot say
deltas?: [{ path, value }] the datamodel writes the step establishes;
every path is declared in ../datamodel.json and every value is
a STRING of source text, never a live value
check?:  { label, result: "pass" | "fail", detail? } - the
author's recorded verdict, typed in, never computed
invoke?: PROPOSED (sb-ig4), see below
PROPOSED STEP FIELD - `invoke` (sb-ig4, 2026-08-28). Flagged the way the
spike flags core.invoke and core.raise themselves: this is the spike's
proposal for how a replay says a step CALLED THE HOST, not a shape any
accepted record defines.
invoke: {
block:    the id of the core.invoke block the call belongs to. The pane
highlights that card's badge for the length of the step, which
is the one thing a reader could not otherwise see: the step
left the chart
outcome:  "done" | "error" - what the host answered
payload?: { name: value } display-only lines, the same string-of-source
-text rule the deltas hold to. Nothing reads them back
The honest-replayer rule applies to `invoke` exactly as it does to
everything else here, and it is worth stating because this is the field
most likely to be mistaken for machinery: on `"outcome": "error"` the
runner does NOT walk the block's on_error subtree. The NEXT step's `active`
is authored - a human wrote those ids after reading the document - and the
pane replays it. `deltas` are applied by the pane's ordinary accumulator on
an error step as on any other; an error step simply tends to write less.
See run_cp_invoke_error below, whose steps 7-8 are authored to sit inside
blk_cp_authorize's on_error subtree and would be just as authored if they
sat anywhere else.
`invoke` ALSO carries a core.subchart step (sb-7s2). The field is reused
rather than joined by a second one because the two say the same thing: the
step left this chart and something else is answering. `block` then names a
core.subchart block, `outcome` is still done|error, and the payload lines
are still display-only strings. What a subchart step does NOT get is any
replay of the CHILD chart - the spike opens one document at a time, so a
child's steps are not stepped through here, and a run that pretended to
would be claiming machinery the D4 ruling refuses. How a child chart's
several final states would map onto a parent's slots is open upstream, and
js/proposed-core.js's sketch says so; these runs use the two outcomes an
invoke has because that is all the vocabulary decides today.

runs.name: Approved and captured
runs.description: The happy path: validation passes, all three lanes clear, the outcome branch takes the approved arm, and the capture succeeds first try.

check.label: arm_valid was taken
check.detail: validation.passed AND amount_cents > 0 AND card.active all held.

steps.label: Two lanes run side by side
steps.note: The parallel block is live: the fraud lane is rating the transaction while the balance lane checks funds. Both cards are highlighted on the canvas.

steps.label: The 3DS lane joins
steps.note: Three lanes active at once - the widest the parallel gets in this run.

check.label: the 3DS group resumed rather than timing out
check.detail: The completion event reached the interrupt rail before the PT10M wait ran out.

steps.label: Risk branch takes the low-risk arm

check.label: arm_low_risk was taken, not arm_high_risk
check.detail: risk_rating 34 < 40 and customer.verified held, so the high-risk arm never armed.

check.label: arm_approved was taken
check.detail: auth.approved AND fraud.cleared AND balance.available_cents >= amount_cents.

check.label: the retry arm was not taken
check.detail: auth.captured == false no longer held, so the one-armed retry branch fell through.

steps.label: Build and send the receipt
steps.note: The tail runs to completion.

runs.name: Fraud flags it for manual review
runs.description: The rating comes back high, the high-risk arm flags a human, and the outcome branch parks the work in the resumable group until a reviewer resolves it two days later.

steps.label: The fraud and balance lanes run together
Risk branch takes the high-risk arm

check.label: arm_high_risk was taken
check.detail: risk_rating 88 >= 70, so the first arm matched before the low-risk arm was tried.

check.label: arm_manual_review was taken, not arm_declined
check.detail: fraud.verdict == 'review' and the backlog was under 50, and arm_declined's guard wanted verdict 'decline'.

steps.label: Two days pass
steps.note: The resumable group holds deep history, so a resume lands back here rather than at the top of the arm.

check.label: the guarded interrupt rule fired
check.detail: decision == 'approve' AND review.parked both held.

runs.name: Customer cancels mid-authorization
runs.description: The customer cancels while the three lanes are still running. The authorization group's guarded interrupt rule abandons the work before anything is captured.

steps.label: The fraud and 3DS lanes are both waiting
steps.note: Two lanes held open at once - this is the step the interrupt lands on.

check.label: the guarded rule fired and the group abandoned
check.detail: reason == 'customer_request' AND auth.captured == false both held, so the rule took its abandon outcome.

steps.label: Tell ops no outcome arm matched
steps.note: The abandon skips the outcome arms, so the otherwise arm carries the notification.

runs.name: 3DS never completes
runs.description: The cardholder never answers the challenge. This fixture expects the PT15M authorization timeout to abandon the group - and the scripted run shows it does not, because the timeout rule's guard reads fraud.cleared, which the fraud lane never set either way.

steps.label: The 3DS wait runs out
steps.note: PT10M elapses with no completion event on the rail.

check.label: the 3DS group did not resume
check.detail: No card.three_ds_completed event arrived, so the wait ran to its end.

steps.label: The PT15M authorization timeout should fire

check.label: the timeout rule abandons the authorization group
check.detail: The rule's guard is three_ds.completed == false OR fraud.cleared == false. The fraud lane never ran, so fraud.cleared is unset rather than false - and this fixture records that the rule did not fire. Whether an unset boolean should read as false is a question for the expression language, not for this pane.

steps.label: The group is still open
steps.note: The run stops here: with nothing on the rail able to fire, the authorization group has no way out.

runs.name: Both host calls answer
runs.description: The two core.invoke steps in their ordinary case: the host answers the authorization, the outcome branch approves, the host answers the capture, and the receipt goes out. Neither on_error subtree is entered, which is the baseline the failure run below is read against.

steps.label: The fraud and balance lanes clear
Authorize the card
steps.note: The card's badge lights while this step is current: the work is happening at the acquirer, not in the chart. Its result is declared to land in `authorization` (core.invoke's assign_to), and ../datamodel.json declares no such entry - so the run writes only the paths the datamodel does declare and leaves the gap visible rather than inventing one. A Phase-B finding, not something a fixture gets to decide.

check.label: the on_error subtree never armed
check.detail: The call answered, so blk_cp_authz_error and the two steps under it are not part of this run at all. Recorded by the author; nothing here evaluated the call.

check.label: arm_approved was taken
check.detail: auth.approved AND fraud.cleared AND balance.available_cents >= amount_cents - and the first of those three is the fact the authorization call established.

steps.label: Capture the funds
steps.note: The second core.invoke, whose on_error slot holds a single park step rather than a sequence. Same badge, same highlight, a smaller failure path.

check.label: neither failure idiom fired
check.detail: The on_error slot is unused because the call answered, and blk_cp_capture_retry's arm is unarmed because auth.captured == false no longer holds. The two idioms are independent, which is the comparison the document exists to make.

steps.label: Build and send the receipt
steps.note: The tail runs to completion.

runs.name: The authorization call fails
runs.description: The other outcome. The fraud lane has already flagged the transaction when the host fails to answer the authorization; the on_error subtree parks it and tells ops, the outcome branch then routes it to the manual-review group, and a reviewer resolves it two days later. Every step after the failure is AUTHORED - the runner replays the ids a human wrote, it does not walk the on_error subtree itself.

steps.label: The fraud and balance lanes run together
Risk branch takes the high-risk arm

check.label: arm_high_risk was taken
check.detail: risk_rating 91 >= 70, so the first arm matched before the low-risk arm was tried.

steps.label: The authorization call fails
steps.note: The badge lights on the same card as in the run above, and the outcome is the difference. What the failure would compile to is proposed-core.js's account: a transition on statifier-ex ADR-0068's error.communication.invoke.blk_cp_authorize into the on_error subtree. Nothing here compiles or fires anything - the next two steps are ids an author wrote down.

check.label: the failure edge is the on_error slot, not a predicate
check.detail: This is failure idiom A: the acquirer never answered, so there is nothing in the datamodel a guard could have read. Idiom B further down the document (blk_cp_capture_retry) could not have caught this one at all.

steps.label: Queue it for review
steps.note: First step inside blk_cp_authorize's on_error subtree, under the core.sequence the zero_or_one slot needs to hold two steps. Authored, not walked.

steps.label: Outcome branch takes arm_manual_review
steps.note: What happens once the on_error subtree finishes - whether the enclosing group carries on to the next step as it does here, and how that reconciles with ADR-0004's single-final emission - is undecided. This run assumes it does carry on, and says so rather than letting the assumption ride as a rendered fact.

check.label: arm_manual_review was taken, not arm_approved
check.detail: fraud.verdict == 'review' and the backlog was under 50. arm_approved wanted auth.approved, which the call that failed never set - an unset boolean, which is the same question run_cp_three_ds_timeout parks for the expression language.

steps.label: Park it for a reviewer
steps.note: The second park of the run, and a different block: blk_cp_authz_park queued the acquirer failure, and this one is the manual-review group's own park inside the resumable group.

steps.label: Two days pass
steps.note: The resumable group holds deep history, so a resume lands back here rather than at the top of the arm.

check.label: the guarded interrupt rule fired
check.detail: decision == 'approve' AND review.parked both held - and review.parked was written by the on_error park, five steps back.

tables.name: Risk rating branch
tables.description: Which arm the fraud lane's branch takes. The arms are tried in order, so a row that satisfies both takes the first.

rows.name: Flagged for review
rows.note: Both arms' expressions hold. The high-risk arm is declared first, so it wins - which is the reason arm order is part of the config and not an implementation detail.

rows.name: Middling, unverified
rows.note: The gap between 40 and 70 is what the otherwise arm exists for.

rows.name: Low but unverified
rows.note: The AND is the whole difference: a low rating alone does not clear the arm.

tables.name: Customer-cancelled interrupt rule
tables.description: Whether the authorization group's cancellation rule fires. It guards on the event payload and on whether the money has already moved.

rows.name: Customer asked, already captured
rows.note: The guard's whole job: once the funds have moved, cancelling is a refund and not an abandon.

rows.name: Cancelled by timeout
rows.note: A timeout cancellation is the other rule's business - this one only answers a deliberate customer request.

tables.name: Outcome branch
tables.description: Three arms over the authorization result, tried in declaration order.

columns.label: Approved
columns.expr: auth.approved AND fraud.cleared AND balance.available_cents >= amount_cents

rows.name: Review queue is full
rows.note: No arm holds, so the otherwise arm notifies ops. A backlog cap that silently changes which arm is taken is exactly the kind of thing a truth table is for.

runs.name: Business plan signup
runs.description: The account is collected, the email verifies inside the day, and the plan branch routes to the company-details step.

check.label: the group resumed rather than waiting out PT24H
arm_business was taken
check.detail: plan == 'business' AND seats > 1.

runs.name: Verification never arrives
runs.description: The customer never opens the email. This fixture expects the wizard to abandon; the scripted run records the PT24H wait falling through with no rule taking it, which is the gap the findings pane already warns about.

steps.label: The wait runs out
steps.note: PT24H with neither signup.email_verified nor signup.abandoned on the rail.

check.label: the verify group ends without a resolution
check.detail: Both interrupt rules wait for an event that never comes, and the group's body has run out. The document needs a timeout rule here - which is what the info-level finding on this group already says.

runs.name: No plan is chosen
runs.description: The other half of the interrupt story: a step RAISES the event a rail is waiting for. A one-seat business plan matches neither arm, so the branch takes otherwise, the nudge goes out, and the proposed core.raise raises signup.abandoned - which the group the branch sits in catches, so the workspace is never provisioned.

steps.label: Plan branch falls through to otherwise

check.label: neither arm holds, so otherwise is taken
check.detail: arm_business needs seats > 1 and arm_personal needs plan == 'personal'. This is the truth table's 'Business, single seat' row, and it is the row whose note calls the outcome probably wrong.

steps.label: Nudge them to pick a plan
Raise signup.abandoned
steps.note: The proposed core.raise. Nothing joins this card to the rail that catches it - they name the same event, and the innermost enclosing group is the one that hears it.

check.label: the raised name matches a rule on the enclosing group's rail
check.detail: Walked by hand when the fixture was written, which is exactly the check an editor-side finding should be making instead.

steps.label: The onboarding group's rail catches it

check.label: the onboarding rail catches it, not the verify group's identical rule
check.detail: The verify group names signup.abandoned too, but it finished several steps ago; a rail only catches while its own group is live.

check.label: provisioning never runs
check.detail: blk_su_provision sits inside the abandoned group, which is why the group wraps the branch and the provisioning step together rather than the branch alone.

tables.name: Plan branch
tables.description: Which onboarding step a new account is routed to.

rows.name: Business, single seat
rows.note: A one-seat business plan falls to the otherwise arm, which nudges them to pick a plan again. Probably wrong, and only visible as a row.

_comment: sb-7s2. The subchart document's runs: one where the child chart comes
back done and one where it comes back error and the on_error subtree
takes over. No `tables` section, and the omission is not an oversight -
this document has no condition-bearing block in it, so there is no
truth table to write and an empty one would only claim otherwise.

runs.name: The invitee signs up
runs.description: The happy path for a child chart: invitations go out, the signup wizard runs as a subchart, it comes back done, and the team is confirmed. The child chart's own steps are not replayed here - the runner opens one document at a time.

steps.label: The child chart is running
steps.note: The subchart card is the active one and the whole child chart is behind it. Nothing here steps into it: the spike opens one document at a time, and a run that walked the child's blocks would be replaying a second document's ids under this one's name.

steps.label: The child chart comes back done

check.label: the outcome lands where assign_to names
check.detail: assign_to is `onboarding`, which ../datamodel.json does not declare - the same undeclared-target finding sb-ig4 found on an invoke and sb-c2o owns. Recorded as a passing check because the replay is honest about what the block says; the finding belongs to the editor, not to this fixture.

steps.label: Give the rest of the team a day
Confirm the team is set up

check.label: the parent carries on after the child finishes
check.detail: A subchart that answers done is a step that finished, so the sequence moves to the next card. That is the uncontroversial half; the error half below is where the open question is.

runs.name: The invitee never finishes
runs.description: The other outcome. The child chart comes back error, the subchart's on_error subtree tells the account owner and raises signup.abandoned, and the group the subchart sits in catches it. Every step after the failure is AUTHORED - the runner replays ids a human wrote after reading the document; it does not walk the on_error subtree itself.

steps.label: The child chart comes back error
steps.note: The badge lights on the same card as in the run above, and the outcome is the difference. What the failure would compile to is proposed-core.js's sketch: a transition on statifier-ex ADR-0068's error.communication.invoke.blk_si_invitee_signup into the on_error subtree. Nothing here compiles or fires anything - the next three steps are ids an author wrote down.

check.label: a child chart's failure is the on_error slot, not a new shape
check.detail: The subchart declares core.invoke's slot unchanged, so the failure path an author draws is the one they already know. What is NOT decided is the other direction: a child chart can finish in several final states, and flattening those to done|error is the open question this fixture parks rather than answers.

steps.label: Tell the account owner
steps.note: First step inside blk_si_invitee_signup's on_error subtree, under the core.sequence the zero_or_one slot needs to hold two steps. Authored, not walked.

steps.label: Raise signup.abandoned
steps.note: The proposed core.raise, the same wiring signup-wizard.json uses. Nothing joins this card to the rail that catches it - they name the same event, and the innermost enclosing group is the one that hears it.

check.label: the raised name matches a rule on the enclosing group's rail
check.detail: Walked by hand when the fixture was written, which is exactly the check an editor-side finding should be making instead.

steps.label: The onboarding group's rail catches it

check.label: a raise from inside a failure subtree is caught like any other
check.detail: The raise sits three levels down, inside the subchart's on_error sequence, and the rail that catches it belongs to the group the subchart sits in. Depth changes nothing: the innermost enclosing group hears it.

steps.label: The onboarding group abandons
steps.note: Where this run stops. Whether the root sequence then carries on to blk_si_confirm is the SAME undecided question run_cp_invoke_error parks - what an enclosing container does once a failure path finishes, and how that reconciles with ADR-0004's single-final emission. This fixture declines to answer it by replaying an answer, so it ends here rather than authoring a confirm step nobody has decided happens.

check.label: the team is not confirmed on this path
check.detail: blk_si_confirm is never activated by this run. That is the fixture's claim and nothing more - it is not evidence about what the compiler would emit.
